items.title: Wendy Oxenhorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 22, 2026
items.q: And Herb Storfer, the original founder who I love, he was the 80-year-old who could no longer help the musicians.

ctx.x: It’s beyond. And we know all the earlier racism, everyone knows the clubs, the labels, the record companies, we know so many things that went down back then. There was one story that really stands out in my early moments, and I’ll segue into the Great Night in Harlem and answer your question, but there was a legend who – I think it was Ron Carter who came to me and said, “I ran into someone at the airport and he didn’t have a seeing eye cane but he was blind as a bat, he really couldn’t see where he was going.”…

coming back and I introduced him, I asked him to do a gig with this young musician and they got tight. And before we knew it young musicians were asking him to sit in at clubs. So he would guest star. So he was making money. They were getting paid more because they had the famous name and they were becoming like family. So this became a little thing that started happening with some of the elders. So many beautiful things. So okay, Great Night in Harlem. I really didn’t know anything about jazz. In fact I could…

was like this is incredible. “I’m going to give you my top producer.” And he gave us Rick White which was amazing, and Dan Melnick. And then some of the guys on our board, Bob Cranshaw and Jimmy Owens, they started reaching out to musicians. At the time I asked if anyone knew anyone famous. Someone had the number for Bill Cosby’s agent, so I left word. I remember a week later I get a call and I hear this guy with this voice that sounds familiar go, “Wendy?” I was like, “Yes.” He goes, “This is Cos.” Okay. This is…

items.title: Wendy Oxenhorn — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Herb Storfer was there, and Ben Giordano.

ctx.x: He lived in Camden, I think.

That’s right. He said, “I’d really love you to check on him. Here’s his number.” I said, “Of course, Ron.” So I checked on Cecil. I called him up, and we started talking. At first he was like, “I don’t need any help; I’m doing just fine.” So we started talking “Train Station Blues,” and I told him about my history playing harmonica in the train stations. That’s actually... By the way, I’m going to segue, because we didn’t catch how I got the job. I was the only one who showed up for the job, the Jazz Foundation…
Thank you. Now back to Cecil Payne.
